Session 4 · 4.1 From localhost to production · 1/2Book ↗

Deploying, and the three environments

EnvironmentWho uses itPurpose
DevelopmentEach programmer, own machineWrite and try code; break things
StagingThe team, testersPrivate replica of production to check a release
ProductionReal customersThe actual business; real, protected data
  • Deployment: putting a version where real users can reach it
  • "It works on my machine" is why staging exists
Session 4 · 4.1 From localhost to production · 2/2Book ↗

Uptime and latency

UptimeDowntime per yearTypical of
99%About 3.7 daysHobby site on one cheap server
99.9%About 8.8 hoursSmall business with sensible hosting
99.99%About 53 minutesPayments, banking, large SaaS
99.999%About 5 minutesTelecom; very expensive
Each extra nine costs dramatically more. Latency: users notice anything over ~100 ms.
Session 4 · 4.2 Step 1: everything on one server · 1/2Book ↗

Rent one computer and install everything

  • A VPS for 5 to 50 dollars a month, running Linux: web server (Nginx) + Python app + PostgreSQL
  • Enough for tens of thousands of visits a day
Session 4 · 4.2 Step 1: everything on one server · 2/2Book ↗

Why it eventually breaks

  • Single point of failure: disk dies, site and data vanish together
  • Resource contention: a heavy report query slows the website for everyone
  • Hard ceiling: the only upgrade is a bigger machine
  • Security blast radius: break into the web server, you are sitting on the customer data
Take each next step when the problem is real, not before.
Session 4 · 4.3 Step 2: the database gets its own machine · 1/2Book ↗

Separate the data tier

  • The database server sits on a private network; a firewall lets only the web server connect
  • No path from the internet to the data
Session 4 · 4.3 Step 2: the database gets its own machine · 2/2Book ↗

Why the second bill is worth it

  • Right-sized hardware: databases want memory and fast disks; web servers want cores and bandwidth
  • Security: a second wall for an attacker; nobody stumbles across the records from outside
  • Independent maintenance: rebuild the web server without touching a byte of data
  • It unlocks Step 3: many web servers sharing one database
  • In practice: a managed database (RDS, Supabase, Neon) with backups, patches, and failover done for you
Session 4 · 4.4 Step 3: many web servers behind a load balancer · 1/3Book ↗

Two ways to add capacity

  • Vertical scaling: a bigger machine. Simple; a ceiling; still one of it
  • Horizontal scaling: more identical machines. No ceiling in principle; losing one is survivable
Session 4 · 4.4 Step 3: many web servers behind a load balancer · 2/3Book ↗

Horizontal scaling with a load balancer

  • The load balancer owns the public address and spreads requests; health checks skip a dead server
Session 4 · 4.4 Step 3: many web servers behind a load balancer · 3/3Book ↗

The catch: servers must be stateless

  • Dana logs in on server 1; her next click lands on server 2, which has never heard of her
  • Stateless servers remember nothing between requests; shared facts live in the database or Redis
  • Interchangeable servers can be added at 9 a.m. and removed after lunch: costs become elastic
  • Duplicates at every layer = high availability: how three and four nines are bought
Ask before launch: "Can we run two copies of this?"
Session 4 · 4.5 Step 4: caches, CDNs, and storage · 1/2Book ↗

Four more components

  • Cache: a fast temporary copy of something expensive (a product list in Redis for 60 seconds). Hard problem: staleness
  • CDN: copies of images, CSS, JS in hundreds of cities; Singapore gets the image from Singapore
  • Object storage (S3): unlimited files by URL; uploads never live on a web server's disk
  • Read replica: a live copy of the database that answers reads and stands by as a spare
Session 4 · 4.5 Step 4: caches, CDNs, and storage · 2/2Book ↗

The standard architecture of a serious web product

  • Still three tiers: each one now duplicated, cached, or moved closer to the user

Session 4 · 4.6 The cloud menu · 2/2Book ↗

Containers, and the advice for this course

  • A container (Docker) packages a program with everything it needs, so it runs identically everywhere
  • Kubernetes runs thousands of containers; almost never the right first choice for a small team
  • For a Claude Code prototype: a PaaS plus a managed database, 0 to 50 dollars a month, no servers to log into
Session 4 · 4.7 Shipping code safelyBook ↗

How code reaches customers

  • Version control (Git, GitHub): every change recorded and reversible
  • CI/CD: tests run on every change; if they pass, it deploys. Small, frequent, low-risk releases
  • Monitoring and logs: find out about outages before customers do
